\title{Boundary-Supported Splitting for Agricultural Field Delineation}
\author{Aviskar~Giri and Isaac~Corley%
\thanks{The authors are with Taylor Geospatial, St.\ Louis, MO 63108 USA
(e-mail: aviskar.giri@taylorgeospatial.org).}}
\markboth{IEEE Geoscience and Remote Sensing Letters}%
{Giri and Corley: Boundary-Supported Splitting for Agricultural Field Delineation}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Field boundary networks predict background, field, and boundary classes, and a marker-controlled watershed on the field class turns the prediction into parcels.
We measure two failures of this conversion on Fields of The World.
Pixels won by the boundary class are dropped from the foreground, which removes thin and small parcels.
The watershed cuts fields at geometric necks that carry no boundary evidence, so its instances score worse than their union.
We propose a post-processing rule that takes every non-background pixel as foreground and keeps a watershed split only where the network's boundary probability exceeds its field probability along most of the split line.
The rule compares the network's own class probabilities, uses three constants that are the same for every country and sensor, and needs no reference polygons.
On ten held-out countries it raises panoptic quality by \GainMin{} to \GainMax{} points over the released pipeline given the same minimum-size step, for two encoders and two sensors, PlanetScope and Sentinel-2.
It improves \UpTotal{} of 40 country and model pairs, with the largest gains on parcels under 0.5~ha.
\end{abstract}

\begin{IEEEkeywords}
Agricultural field delineation, instance segmentation, watershed transform, post-processing, remote sensing.
\end{IEEEkeywords}

\section{Introduction}
\IEEEPARstart{F}{ield} polygons are the unit at which crop area, yield, and management practices are reported, so a field boundary model is only useful once its pixel predictions become one polygon per parcel.
Public benchmarks now cover this task at 10~m with Sentinel-2~\cite{kerner2024ftw,dandrimont2023ai4boundaries,persello2023ai4smallfarms}, at 3~m with PlanetScope~\cite{corley_ftp}, and at global scale~\cite{ftw_global}, and the models trained on them predict three classes, background, field interior, and boundary~\cite{waldner2020decode,waldner2020edge,kerner2024ftw,muhawenayo2026prue}.
The released pipelines convert this map with a marker-controlled watershed~\cite{soille2004morphological} in which field pixels form the mask, the distance to the nearest predicted boundary pixel forms the surface, and $h$-maxima of that distance seed the flood~\cite{waldner2020decode,corley_ftp}.
Adjacent instances are then merged into connected components before polygons are extracted.
The same conversion is used at continental scale~\cite{ftw_global}, so its errors carry into the parcel counts derived from it.

Two properties of this conversion cost accuracy (Fig.~\ref{fig:gallery}).
First, the field mask excludes every pixel the boundary class wins.
Where a parcel is narrow or its edges are uncertain, the boundary class covers it and the parcel disappears.
In our evaluation \BaseMiss\% of reference parcels have no prediction covering half of their area, and the released pipeline predicts \BaseBiasAbs{} fewer parcels per patch than the reference.
Second, the watershed places its lines at geometric necks of the mask.
Whether a neck coincides with a predicted boundary is never checked, and scoring the watershed instances gives \RawInstPQ{} panoptic quality against \CCPQ{} for the plain connected components of the same mask.
Merging the instances back recovers the accuracy, which is what the released pipelines do, but it also discards every correct split.

We change the conversion in two places.
The foreground becomes every pixel that is not background, so boundary pixels stay inside the parcels they border.
The watershed then runs with lines, and a line is kept only if at least a fraction $\tau$ of its pixels have boundary probability at least equal to field probability, and otherwise the two regions merge.
The split test compares two outputs of the same network at the same pixel, so it does not depend on probability calibration.
The marker depth stays at the released default of $h=2$.
A minimum parcel size, which any conversion can apply, removes the smallest polygons at the end.
All three constants are the same for every country and sensor.

We evaluate on the ten densely annotated held-out countries of Fields of The World v2~\cite{kerner2024ftw} with the released EfficientNet~\cite{tan2019efficientnet} U-Nets~\cite{ronneberger2015unet} for PlanetScope~\cite{corley_ftp} and Sentinel-2~\cite{kerner2024ftw}, scored against the vector parcels.
The rule raises macro panoptic quality by \GainMin{} to \GainMax{} points over the released pipeline given the same minimum-size step, for two encoders and two sensors, and improves \UpTotal{} of the 40 country and model pairs.
Selecting the best watershed depth per country on the test labels recovers less than a third of that gain (Sec.~\ref{sec:results}).

\section{Related Work}
Field delineation from satellite imagery has moved from edge detection and region growing~\cite{wagner2020growing} to fully convolutional networks that predict boundary and interior classes~\cite{persello2019delineation,waldner2020decode,waldner2020edge} and, most recently, to benchmark datasets that fix the annotation and the evaluation~\cite{kerner2024ftw,dandrimont2023ai4boundaries,persello2023ai4smallfarms,corley_ftp}.
PRUE~\cite{muhawenayo2026prue} compared encoders, decoders, and training recipes on Fields of The World and found that a U-Net with an EfficientNet encoder remains the most accurate choice.
Fields of the Planet~\cite{corley_ftp} reports that these three-class networks outperform the Delineate Anything instance models~\cite{lavreniuk2025delineateanything}, in both their first and second versions, on the same held-out countries.
Polygon extraction with frame fields or graph networks has been studied for buildings~\cite{girard2021framefield,zorzi2022polyworld,zorzi2020regularization}, but the released field models on these benchmarks remain three-class semantic networks followed by a watershed.
We evaluate on those released networks, so an improvement in their conversion to polygons applies to the current best models without retraining.

Hierarchical segmentation orders contours by strength and thresholds the hierarchy~\cite{arbelaez2011hierarchical,maninis2018cob}, and Persello et al.~\cite{persello2019delineation} apply this grouping to field contours.
Stochastic watershed estimates contour probability by resampling markers~\cite{angulo2007stochastic}, and iterative $h$-minima methods adapt the marker depth per object~\cite{koyuncu2016iterative}.
These methods decide splits from the geometry of one surface or from marker statistics.
We instead test each watershed line against a second network output, the boundary probability, so the split decision uses evidence the surface does not contain.
We also change the foreground so that pixels of that boundary class are not discarded.
Test-time augmentation~\cite{wang2019tta} and ensembling~\cite{lakshminarayanan2017deepensembles} average the class probabilities and are already part of the released inference, and our rule reads the averaged output.

\section{Method}
\label{sec:method}
The input is the softmax output $p_{\mathrm{bg}}, p_{\mathrm{field}}, p_{\mathrm{bnd}}$ of a three-class network on one image, and the output is a set of field polygons (Fig.~\ref{fig:pipeline}).
Only the argmax and the two class probabilities at each pixel are used.

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{rev_method.pdf}
\caption{\textbf{Every intermediate image on one PlanetScope crop.}
(a) Image. (b) Boundary probability from the network. (c) Foreground: the released pipeline keeps the green pixels only; we also keep the orange boundary pixels. (d) Distance to the predicted boundary with the $h$-maxima markers. (e) Watershed regions and the lines between them. (f) Each line colored by its support $s(\ell)$, the fraction of its pixels where $p_{\mathrm{bnd}}\geq p_{\mathrm{field}}$; blue lines ($s\geq\tau$) are kept and red lines are merged. (g) Resulting parcels with the reference outlined.}
\label{fig:pipeline}
\end{figure*}

\paragraph{Foreground}
The foreground mask is $F=\{\arg\max p \neq \mathrm{bg}\}$, the union of the field and boundary classes.
The released pipelines use the field class alone, which removes a parcel whenever the boundary class covers it.
In our evaluation this rule alone, without any splitting, merges neighboring parcels into single components and lowers panoptic quality to \NbgNonePQ{}, so the foreground change is only useful together with a split rule that can separate the parcels the boundary pixels now connect.

\paragraph{Split proposals}
Let $D$ be the Euclidean distance from each pixel to the nearest pixel with $\arg\max p = \mathrm{bnd}$, set to zero outside $F$.
The $h$-maxima of $D$ with $h=2$ pixels are the markers, and a watershed of $-D$ restricted to $F$ produces regions separated by one-pixel lines~\cite{soille2004morphological}.
This is the released procedure with the mask replaced by $F$ and with lines retained.
The watershed over-segments by design, because it cuts at every neck of the mask, and the next step decides which cuts to keep.

\paragraph{Boundary-supported merging}
Each line $\ell$ separates two regions.
Its support is the fraction of its pixels at which the network favors boundary over field,
\begin{equation}
s(\ell)=\frac{1}{|\ell|}\sum_{x\in\ell}\mathbf{1}\left[p_{\mathrm{bnd}}(x)\geq p_{\mathrm{field}}(x)\right],
\label{eq:support}
\end{equation}
where $\mathbf{1}[\cdot]$ is the indicator function.
A line with $s(\ell)\geq\tau$ is kept as a one-pixel gap and the two regions become separate parcels.
A line with $s(\ell)<\tau$ is removed and the two regions merge.
All line decisions are applied together with a union-find, and a line pixel is filled only when every region it touches ends up in the same group and no neighboring line pixel would be filled with a different one.
A kept line therefore stays a one-pixel gap, and each connected group of foreground pixels becomes one parcel.
We use $\tau=0.7$; values from 0.7 to 0.9 change the result by less than half a point (Sec.~\ref{sec:ablation}).

\paragraph{Polygons}
Each parcel becomes one polygon from its pixel boundary, without simplification, and the one-pixel gaps keep neighbors distinct when the polygons are rasterized on the same grid.
Parcels smaller than 900~m$^2$ are then dropped, with the threshold chosen on the validation split.
It is given in ground area rather than pixels so that it means the same on either sensor.
This last step is not specific to our rule, and Sec.~\ref{sec:ablation} reports it for the released pipeline as well.

The rule keeps a split only where the network predicted a boundary along most of the seam, which closes gaps in thin or broken boundaries, and merges the geometric splits that have no such evidence.
Sec.~\ref{sec:compare} measures what per-country tuning of $h$ and $\tau$ would add.

\section{Experiments}
\label{sec:experiments}

\paragraph{Data}
We use the test split of the ten densely annotated held-out countries of Fields of The World v2~\cite{kerner2024ftw}, named in Fig.~\ref{fig:percountry}, with 2,544 PlanetScope patches at 3~m~\cite{corley_ftp} and 3,034 Sentinel-2 patches.
Kenya is excluded because its annotations are presence-only.
The PlanetScope set is the subset of these patches with a co-registered PlanetScope image, so each sensor is compared against its own baseline rather than against the other.
The reference for every score is the released vector parcels clipped to each patch, not the rasterized semantic mask.

\paragraph{Models}
The models are the EfficientNet-B3 and B7 U-Nets of Fields of the Planet for PlanetScope~\cite{corley_ftp} and of Fields of The World for Sentinel-2~\cite{kerner2024ftw}, run from the released checkpoints with the released inference settings, including eight-fold flip and rotation averaging.
Sentinel-2 chips are distributed on a 256$\times$256 grid per patch, so their ground sampling varies with latitude.
Following the released evaluation we upsample by two and score on that grid, and no weights are changed.

\paragraph{Baselines}
The released pipeline takes the field argmax, runs the watershed at $h=2$, and extracts connected components of the union of instances.
Our implementation reproduces the per-country panoptic quality reported for PlanetScope~\cite{corley_ftp} to within $10^{-3}$, and the same for Sentinel-2~\cite{kerner2024ftw} under the native-resolution scoring of that paper.
The best single depth selects, for each country, the depth in $\{0.5,\ldots,64\}$ with the highest test score under the same procedure.
It uses the test labels, so it bounds what depth tuning can achieve.
We also implement four prior conversions on the same predictions: extent and boundary thresholds~\cite{waldner2020decode}, hierarchical merging of an over-segmentation by mean boundary probability along each shared border~\cite{arbelaez2011hierarchical,maninis2018cob,persello2019delineation}, stochastic watershed with random markers~\cite{angulo2007stochastic}, and iterative marker depth~\cite{koyuncu2016iterative}.
We sweep each over its own grid and report on test the setting with the highest macro score on the \emph{validation} split, the same rule we use for ours.

\paragraph{Metrics}
We match predicted and reference polygons greedily at intersection over union 0.5.
Every method compared here returns a partition of the foreground, so no two predictions overlap and the matching does not depend on the order they are visited in.
Recognition quality (RQ) is the object F1, segmentation quality (SQ) the mean matched IoU, and panoptic quality (PQ) their product~\cite{kirillov2019panoptic}, pooled over the patches of a country and averaged over the ten countries.
PQ$_{\mathrm{s}}$ is PQ over reference parcels under 0.5~ha.
The miss rate is the fraction of reference parcels with no prediction covering half of their area, and the merge rate the fraction of predictions covering half of two or more reference parcels.
All values are on a 0--100 scale.

\subsection{Results}
\label{sec:results}
Our rule raises PQ on all four model and sensor pairs against the released pipeline given the same minimum-size step (Table~\ref{tab:main}), and the gain is larger than what selecting the best watershed depth per country on the test labels can reach.
Against the released pipeline as published, without that step, the gain is \GainPubPlanetThree{} points on PlanetScope B3.
SQ, RQ, and small-parcel PQ rise together, the merge rate is almost unchanged, and the miss rate drops on every pair, so the gain comes from parcels that re-enter the foreground and not from splitting the same mask differently.
Cambodia, where parcels are smallest, gains most, and Portugal, with two test patches, is the only pair that decreases (Fig.~\ref{fig:percountry}).
At the patch level the recovered parcels are the thin ones the released pipeline dropped or absorbed into a neighbor, in every country and on both sensors (Fig.~\ref{fig:gallery}).

\subsection{Comparison with Prior Post-Processing}
\label{sec:compare}
No prior conversion reaches the released pipeline on these predictions, and ours is the only one above it (Table~\ref{tab:compare}).
Thresholding the two probability maps is the strongest and the cheapest of them, but a parcel whose shared boundary is broken stays merged, which is the case the watershed exists to handle.
Hierarchical merging is the closest to ours, since it also scores a border by boundary probability, but it ranks borders on an absolute scale and merges until a level is reached, while our test compares two probabilities at the same pixel.
The minimum-size step of Sec.~\ref{sec:method} is applied to every row, and it helps the methods that leave the most fragments the most, without changing the ordering.
Replacing the one shared setting with the best setting for each country, chosen with that country's own test labels, adds \OursTune{} points to ours and at most \PriorTuneMax{} to any prior method, so the ordering does not depend on per-region tuning.
We measure cost on one core, on PlanetScope patches grouped by how many reference parcels they contain.
On Sentinel-2 every method scales with the larger grid and the ordering is unchanged.
Ours adds \OursSlowdown{} over the released pipeline on dense patches, and stochastic watershed, which repeats the flood for every marker draw, is \SwstSlowdown{} slower.
Peak additional memory stays under \PeakMB{}~MB per patch for every method on either sensor, so the choice is about time rather than memory.

\subsection{Ablation}
\label{sec:ablation}
Neither change helps alone (Table~\ref{tab:ablation}).
The wider foreground without a split rule merges neighboring parcels into single components, and the split rule on the field foreground has nothing to add, because the gaps the boundary class already leaves in that mask separate most parcels.
The gain appears only when the boundary pixels are kept and the watershed lines through them are tested.
Over the sweeps in the supplementary material the result is flat for $\tau$ between 0.7 and 0.9 and for $h$ between 1 and 2, and $h=8$ removes the markers of small parcels and loses accuracy.
The alternatives we tried in place of the argmax, a self-adaptive threshold on the field probability, morphological closing of the boundary class, and a watershed on the boundary probability itself, all score below the released pipeline.
Requiring a minimum kept-line length, widening the support test to a tolerance band, filling holes inside a parcel, and merging slivers into a neighbor each lowered the validation score.
The minimum parcel size is the one added step that helps, and it helps the released pipeline as well, by \BaseAreaGain{} points against \OursAreaGain{} for ours, so the ordering is the same with or without it.
The released polygonization tool~\cite{kerner2024ftw} exposes such a threshold, although the published evaluation does not apply one.

\subsection{Qualitative Results}
Fig.~\ref{fig:pipeline} follows one crop through the pipeline.
The orange pixels in panel~(c) are the ones the released mask discards.
They are the narrow strips between fields and along the road, and they return as parcels in panel~(g).
Panel~(f) separates the two kinds of watershed line.
A line that follows a predicted boundary has support near one and is kept, and a line that cuts across a field at a neck has support near zero and is merged.
The failure case in Fig.~\ref{fig:gallery} (last example) shows the limit of the rule.
A track inside a reference parcel is predicted as boundary, the line along it is supported, and the parcel is split.
The rule cannot separate an internal track from a parcel boundary when the network labels both as boundary.

\section{Conclusion}
We keep the boundary class inside the foreground and let it decide which watershed splits are kept.
The two changes together improve polygon accuracy over the released pipeline on two encoders and two sensors with no per-region tuning, and the gain comes from parcels that the field mask had discarded.
The rule requires a predicted boundary class, so it does not apply to instance segmentation outputs that carry masks and scores only, and on Sentinel-2 the recovered parcels are narrower than the 10~m the sensor resolves and survive only on the upsampled prediction grid.
Parcels the network does not detect at all remain missing, and those are now the largest error.
